teaser.text: HSBC is a bank that earns money by moving, lending, investing and protecting it for people, businesses and institutions. Its business becomes clearer when you follow a dollar from a customer’s account through the services HSBC provides, the costs it bears and the profit left over.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for HSBC?

paragraphs.text: The bear case requires lower rates, persistent Hong Kong property stress and a costly Hang Seng integration to weaken earnings and capital.

The bull case requires wealth inflows to become recurring fees, savings to arrive without disruption and Hang Seng synergies to exceed their costs. Credit losses fall toward 30 basis points, capital rebuilds and buybacks strengthen, supporting P/B expansion.

blocks.heading: How much cash does HSBC really make?

paragraphs.text: Industrial-company measures such as net debt to EBITDA and free-cash-flow yield do not fit HSBC because deposits, lending and interest are the operating business itself. Investors should instead test net interest margin, credit losses, RoTE and CET1.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for HSBC today?

paragraphs.text: A share is a small claim on the profit left after HSBC pays depositors, employees, lenders, taxes and credit losses. Its trailing P/E is 13.0x, meaning investors pay £13 for each £1 of recent earnings. The forward P/E is 9.6x, which implies that forecast earnings are higher, although some improvement may simply reflect old charges disappearing.

blocks.heading: How much does HSBC pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise from $0.85 in FY2026 to $0.98 in FY2029. The path starts near the 50% payout target and the $1.90 next-12-month EPS estimate, while the first two 2026 interim dividends already total $0.20. The bear case falls from $0.65 to $0.55 as credit costs and capital pressure persist; the bull case rises from $0.90 to $1.20 as wealth income, savings and Hang Seng synergies strengthen earnings.

blocks.heading: Does HSBC cover its dividend with cash?

paragraphs.text: HSBC’s profit attributable to ordinary shareholders rose from $12,607 million in 2021 to $21,102 million in 2025. Across those years, common dividends and buybacks totalled $76,474 million. The distribution share rose from 41.1% to 98.0%, changing HSBC from a bank that retained substantial earnings into one that returned almost all of them.

HSBC also invested in the continuing business. From 2021 to 2025, it spent about $6.3 billion on property and equipment and $13.9 billion on intangible assets, principally software and other infrastructure. It used subordinated debt, which absorbs losses before senior debt, to manage regulatory capital. Buybacks reduced the number of shares, giving each remaining share a larger claim on future earnings, but that mechanical benefit does not prove every repurchase was made at an attractive price.

paragraphs.text: Management targets RoTE of 17% or better from 2026 through 2028 and revenue growth of 5% in 2028. It targets a 50% dividend payout from adjusted earnings. For 2026, guidance is at least US$46 billion of Banking NII and around 45 basis points of ECL charges. Operating-expense growth is about 1%. HSBC also targets a 14%–14.5% CET1 ratio and around US$2.0 billion of annualised simplification savings by end-2026.

blocks.heading: What is HSBC’s dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: A bank’s deposits are not spare cash. A customer’s deposit is money HSBC owes, while loans and securities are assets that generate income. The important questions are therefore the interest spread, credit losses and capital strength. The 4.1% dividend yield matters because it represents cash returned to shareholders, provided repeatable earnings and surplus capital support it.

blocks.heading: What has HSBC guided for 2026 through 2028?

paragraphs.text: RoTE means return on average tangible equity: profit for ordinary shareholders measured against capital after removing goodwill and other intangible assets. HSBC’s floor is 17% or better. It applies in each year from 2026 through 2028. In the first half of 2026, annualised RoTE was 18.2%, or 19.1% excluding notable items such as restructuring and disposal effects. That explains why the target can differ from reported profit.

Expected credit losses, or ECL, are accounting estimates for loans that may not be fully repaid. HSBC expects around 45 basis points in 2026. That is above its 30–40 basis-point medium-term range. Operating expenses should rise about 1%. It also retains a net-zero-by-2050 ambition. By 2030, it aims to provide or facilitate $750bn–$1tn of sustainable finance and investment.

blocks.heading: Has HSBC kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: HSBC also reports progress on simplification. It says $1.7 billion of annualised savings has been actioned, against $1.4 billion of restructuring costs, and has raised the target to $2 billion. Annualised means the expected yearly saving once changes operate; it is not cash already received. The savings count only if they survive reinvestment, inflation and new costs.

paragraphs.text: Revenue reached US$19,118 million, up 16.1% from the year before. Net interest income also increased, and profit after tax rose far faster because the June 2025 quarter contained BoCom dilution and impairment losses of about US$2.1 billion. Their non-recurrence explains much of the rebound.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in HSBC's next results?

paragraphs.text: HSBC reports third-quarter results on 27 October 2026. Investors should ask whether Banking NII is tracking towards at least $46bn and whether credit losses remain near 45 basis points. They should also compare realised savings with new investment. Higher revenue matters only if the cost of earning and protecting it remains manageable.
